analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid to cover routine care costs for patients joining cancer and other clinical trials.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 61 cosponsors to make Medicaid cover routine care for Medicaid enrollees in life-saving clinical trials died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state Medicaid program to pay the routine costs of care — doctor visits, scans, hospital stays, and treatment for complications — for Medicaid enrollees who join approved clinical trials for cancer or other life-threatening conditions. Today, many Medicaid patients with no other insurance cannot join a trial because Medicaid does not clearly cover the ordinary care they would need while in it. The bill would not have paid for the experimental treatment itself; that is paid for by the trial's sponsor. It never received a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and the Congress ended in January 2021 without the bill moving.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid enrollees with cancer or other life-threatening conditions who want to join an approved clinical trial. Their routine care — the kind of treatment they would need whether or not they were in a trial — would be covered by Medicaid, and coverage decisions would have to be made within 48 hours without restricting which doctor or trial site they could use. The bill would also cover people in the Medicaid expansion population. Researchers and drug developers would also benefit from a larger, more representative pool of trial participants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicaid patients with cancer and serious diseases

how_it_helps.text: Requires state Medicaid programs to cover 'routine patient costs' for Medicaid enrollees in qualifying clinical trials for cancer or other life-threatening conditions — the items and services that would already be covered outside the trial, plus care for trial complications [S2].

The bill excludes the experimental drug or treatment being tested, which the trial sponsor pays for, and excludes items used only for data collection — so the added cost to Medicaid is limited to ordinary care and complication management [S3].
Coverage determinations must be completed within 48 hours, cannot be limited by the provider's location or network, and cannot require trials to submit proprietary or burdensome protocols [S3].
Coverage applies to all state plans and, beginning January 1, 2020, to the Medicaid expansion population [S3].

Qualifying trials include those approved or funded by NIH, CDC, AHRQ, CMS, the Departments of Defense, Veterans Affairs and Energy, peer-reviewed nongovernmental research, and FDA-reviewed drug trials [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State Medicaid programs (and the federal government, which shares Medicaid costs) would pay the routine care costs of enrollees in clinical trials. Because the bill only requires coverage of care patients would already be entitled to outside a trial, plus treatment for complications, the added cost is modest — but it is a new federal mandate on states, and states where legislation is needed would have a grace period to comply.

drawbacks.text: The bill is an unfunded federal mandate: states would have to absorb the added Medicaid costs without new federal money earmarked for them, and the bill allows states extra time (until after their next legislative session) before they must comply [S3].
The bill includes phase I trials, which test very early, unproven treatments and carry the highest risk of complications — care for those complications would fall on Medicaid budgets [S3].
Attestation-based, expedited coverage determinations within 48 hours give state agencies limited ability to scrutinize whether a trial is appropriate for a particular patient [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is careful: Medicaid pays only for care patients would be entitled to anyway, not the experimental treatment itself, which keeps the cost to states modest while removing the insurance barrier that keeps low-income patients out of trials. The main honest cost is that it is an unfunded mandate on state Medicaid budgets, and phase I complications could add expense. On balance, the benefit — access to potentially life-saving trials for patients who otherwise often cannot afford to participate — outweighs a limited, well-defined cost increase.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote — and the two-year Congress ended without the bill reaching the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) introduced the bill on January 30, 2019, joined by Rep. Gus Bilirakis (R-FL), and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
The bill attracted 61 cosponsors, including 9 of the 197 House Republicans and 52 of the 231 House Democrats — bipartisan support spread across both parties [S4].

Despite that bipartisan sponsorship, the Energy and Commerce Committee never scheduled the bill for consideration, and no version of it was ever voted on by the full House during the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State Medicaid budgets and the committee leadership that avoided adding a new mandate to its docket are better off because the bill died; Medicaid enrollees with cancer who cannot join clinical trials are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State Medicaid budgets; the bill's would-be beneficiaries did not benefit

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan — 52 of 231 House Democrats and 9 of 197 House Republicans cosponsored it — and it was never voted on, so no roll call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Drug developers and clinical trial sponsors
industries.note: The bill would have expanded the pool of Medicaid patients able to enroll in clinical trials, giving sponsors more participants and more representative data. This runs alongside patients' interests, since it removes the insurance barrier that kept low-income patients out of trials.
Trial sites and the research community would have seen more enrollment from the Medicaid population, which supports trial recruitment and research funding.

States would bear the new mandate to cover routine care costs for enrollees in trials without dedicated federal funding, though the bill limits covered costs to care patients would already be entitled to outside a trial.
